title: Halfway Between Two Frames
statement: In the coordinate plane, let $A$ be the rectangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(10,0)$, $(10,6)$ and $(0,6)$, and let $B$ be the rectangle with vertices $(20,10)$, $(24,10)$, $(24,12)$ and $(20,12)$. Let $M$ be the set of all midpoints of segments $PQ$, where $P$ is any point on the perimeter of $A$ and $Q$ is any point on the perimeter of $B$. Find the area of $M$.
hints: Take one edge of $A$ and one edge of $B$, and ask what shape the midpoints form as $P$ and $Q$ move along just those two edges. Try a horizontal edge of $A$ with a vertical edge of $B$.

Use casework on the pair of edges containing $P$ and $Q$. Each rectangle has four edges, so there are $16$ pairs. If the two edges are parallel, the midpoints form a segment, which has no area. If they are perpendicular, the two midpoint coordinates vary independently, so the midpoints fill a solid rectangle.

Each midpoint coordinate is the average of a coordinate of $P$ and one of $Q$. Applying this to the perpendicular pairs, the rectangles of midpoints combine into four strips: $5 \le y \le 6$ and $8 \le y \le 9$ with $10 \le x \le 17$, and $10 \le x \le 12$ and $15 \le x \le 17$ with $5 \le y \le 9$. Together they form a frame with a hole in the middle, so find its area by subtracting the hole from the outer rectangle.
solution: Suppose $P$ lies on an edge of $A$ and $Q$ lies on an edge of $B$. If the two edges are parallel, then one coordinate of the midpoint is fixed, so the midpoints lie on a line segment. There are finitely many such segments and they have zero area, so they can be ignored. If the two edges are perpendicular, then one midpoint coordinate depends only on the position of $P$ and the other only on the position of $Q$. These coordinates vary independently, so the midpoints fill a solid rectangle. First let $P = (t, a)$ lie on a horizontal edge of $A$, with $0 \le t \le 10$ and $a \in \{0, 6\}$, and let $Q = (b, s)$ lie on a vertical edge of $B$, with $b \in \{20, 24\}$ and $10 \le s \le 12$. The midpoint is $\left(\frac{t + b}{2}, \frac{a + s}{2}\right)$. Here $x$ fills $[10, 15]$ when $b = 20$ and $[12, 17]$ when $b = 24$, which together make $[10, 17]$. Also $y$ fills $[5, 6]$ when $a = 0$ and $[8, 9]$ when $a = 6$. So these pairs of edges give exactly the two strips $10 \le x \le 17,\ 5 \le y \le 6$ and $10 \le x \le 17,\ 8 \le y \le 9$. Now let $P = (a, t)$ lie on a vertical edge of $A$, with $a \in \{0, 10\}$ and $0 \le t \le 6$, and let $Q = (s, b)$ lie on a horizontal edge of $B$, with $20 \le s \le 24$ and $b \in \{10, 12\}$. The midpoint is $\left(\frac{a + s}{2}, \frac{t + b}{2}\right)$. Here $x$ fills $[10, 12]$ when $a = 0$ and $[15, 17]$ when $a = 10$. Also $y$ fills $[5, 8]$ when $b = 10$ and $[6, 9]$ when $b = 12$, which together make $[5, 9]$. So these pairs give exactly the two strips $10 \le x \le 12,\ 5 \le y \le 9$ and $15 \le x \le 17,\ 5 \le y \le 9$. A point of the rectangle $10 \le x \le 17,\ 5 \le y \le 9$ lies in one of the four strips exactly when $y \le 6$, $y \ge 8$, $x \le 12$ or $x \ge 15$. Hence, apart from the zero-area segments, $M$ is this rectangle with the open rectangle $12 < x < 15,\ 6 < y < 8$ removed. The outer rectangle measures $7$ by $4$ and has area $28$. The hole measures $3$ by $2$ and has area $6$. The area of $M$ is therefore $28 - 6 = 22$. The answer is $22$. Why this works. casework, area-by-decomposition: splitting by the pair of edges turns the set of midpoints into axis-parallel strips, whose union is a rectangle with a rectangular hole.

solution_figures.alt: The set of midpoints drawn as a shaded rectangular frame. The outer rectangle RSTU measures 7 by 4, with R at (10, 5) and T at (17, 9), and the unshaded inner rectangle EFGH measures 3 by 2, with E at (12, 6) and G at (15, 8).
